title: Grammar & Punctuation
description: Essential grammar rules — parts of speech, sentence types, punctuation, common errors, and how grammar choices affect meaning and style.

notes.heading: Parts of Speech
notes.body: Eight parts of speech: Noun (person, place, thing, idea), Pronoun (replaces noun: he, she, it, they), Verb (action or state: run, is, become), Adjective (describes noun: blue, tall, impossible), Adverb (describes verb/adjective/adverb: quickly, very, well), Preposition (shows relationship: in, on, under, between), Conjunction (joins: and, but, because, although), Interjection (exclamation: Oh! Wow! Ouch!). Each word in a sentence belongs to at least one category. Understanding parts of speech helps you: vary sentence structure, identify and fix errors, understand how language works. The same word can function as different parts of speech depending on context: 'run' can be verb (I run) or noun (a fun run).

notes.heading: Sentence Types and Structures
notes.body: Four sentence types: Declarative (statement), Interrogative (question), Imperative (command), Exclamatory (exclamation). Three sentence structures: Simple (one independent clause: 'The dog barked.'), Compound (two+ independent clauses joined by conjunction/semicolon: 'The dog barked, and the cat ran.'), Complex (independent + dependent clause: 'Although the dog barked, the cat stayed.'). Varying sentence structure creates rhythm and emphasis. Too many simple sentences = choppy. Too many long complex sentences = exhausting. Effects: short sentences create urgency/tension. Long sentences create flow and build detail. Deliberate fragments: 'Silence. Complete silence.' — effective for dramatic emphasis when used purposefully.

notes.heading: Punctuation Guide
notes.body: Full stop (.): ends declarative sentences. Comma (,): separates items in lists, clauses, and parenthetical information. Semicolon (;): joins related independent clauses (stronger than comma, weaker than full stop). Colon (:): introduces a list, explanation, or quotation. Apostrophe ('): possession (the girl's book) and contractions (don't = do not). Quotation marks: direct speech or quoted text. Dash (—): emphatic pause or parenthetical information. Hyphen (-): joins compound words. Parentheses (brackets): additional, non-essential information. Ellipsis (...): trailing off, omission, or pause. Common errors: comma splices (joining independent clauses with only a comma — use semicolon or conjunction), its/it's confusion (its = possession; it's = it is), their/there/they're confusion.

notes.heading: Subject-Verb Agreement and Tense
notes.body: Subject and verb must agree in number: singular subject → singular verb ('The dog runs'); plural subject → plural verb ('The dogs run'). Tricky cases: collective nouns ('The team IS winning' — British English sometimes treats as plural: 'The team ARE divided'). Either/or, neither/nor: verb agrees with nearest subject. Tense: indicates time. Past, present, future are the three main tenses, each with simple, continuous, perfect, and perfect continuous aspects. Consistent tense: avoid switching between past and present unintentionally ('She walked in and says hello' → 'She walked in and said hello'). In literary analysis, use PRESENT tense when discussing what happens in a text ('Shakespeare presents...' not 'Shakespeare presented...').

notes.heading: Active and Passive Voice
notes.body: Active voice: subject performs action ('The scientist conducted the experiment'). Direct, clear, concise — generally preferred. Passive voice: subject receives action ('The experiment was conducted by the scientist'). Agent (who did it) can be omitted: 'The experiment was conducted.' Uses: when agent is unknown ('My bike was stolen'), when agent is unimportant ('The roads were repaired'), or in formal/scientific writing to sound objective. Overuse of passive makes writing vague and wordy. Identifying passive: form of 'to be' + past participle ('was eaten,' 'has been decided'). In MYP, active voice is generally preferred unless there's a specific reason for passive.

notes.heading: Common Grammatical Errors
notes.body: Run-on sentences: two+ independent clauses without proper punctuation/conjunction. Fix with full stop, semicolon, or conjunction. Comma splice: joining independent clauses with only a comma. Dangling modifier: modifier doesn't logically attach to anything in the sentence. 'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful.' (Trees don't walk! → 'Walking down the street, I admired the beautiful trees.'). Pronoun ambiguity: unclear what a pronoun refers to. 'When Sarah met Emma, she was excited.' (Who was excited?). Misplaced modifier: modifier in wrong position. 'I only ate pizza' vs 'I ate only pizza' (different meanings). Double negative: 'I don't have none' → 'I don't have any.'

notes.heading: Grammar as a Stylistic Tool
notes.body: Grammar isn't just rules — it's a tool for creating effect. Fragments: 'Alone.' 'Never again.' — emphasis through brevity. Polysyndeton: excessive conjunctions ('We ran and jumped and laughed and cried and lived') — creates energy, overwhelm. Asyndeton: omission of conjunctions ('I came, I saw, I conquered') — creates speed, decisiveness. Parallelism: similar grammatical structure in series ('of the people, by the people, for the people') — creates rhythm and memorability. Authors break grammar rules deliberately for effect — but you must demonstrate you KNOW the rules before you break them. In your own writing, intentional deviation is style; unintentional errors weaken credibility.

flashcards.definition: Describes verb, adjective, or another adverb. Often ends in -ly.
Joins related independent clauses. Stronger than comma, weaker than full stop.
flashcards.example: 'She loves coffee; he prefers tea.' Both halves could be separate sentences.

flashcards.definition: Its = possession (the dog wagged its tail). It's = it is or it has.
flashcards.example: 'It's raining' (it is). 'The cat licked its paw' (possession).

flashcards.definition: Subject performs action. Direct and clear.
flashcards.example: 'The student wrote the essay.' (Active). 'The essay was written by the student.' (Passive).

flashcards.definition: Incorrectly joining two independent clauses with only a comma.
flashcards.example: Wrong: 'I love reading, it relaxes me.' Right: 'I love reading; it relaxes me.'

flashcards.definition: Singular subject + singular verb. Plural subject + plural verb.
Use present tense when discussing events in literature.
flashcards.example: 'Shakespeare presents Macbeth as ambitious.' NOT 'Shakespeare presented...'

flashcards.definition: Similar grammatical structure in a series. Creates rhythm and impact.
flashcards.example: 'I came, I saw, I conquered.' 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.'

flashcards.definition: Introduces a list, explanation, or quotation.
flashcards.example: 'She brought three things: courage, determination, and hope.'
